summary: Zyan prompts Claude Fable 5.2 to formulate reflective interaction nets with introspection capabilities, demonstrating the resulting agent reduction behavior through an interactive web viewer screen recording.
summaryEn: Reflective Interaction Nets Graph Reduction Visualization

post.originalText: Welp, I asked Fable 5.2 for reflective interaction nets, and I suppose it did give me what I asked for but it did it kinda ugly. Looks like it arrived on a solution that has this special "reader" agent that when applied converts a whole subtree into lambda-encoding of that subtree... this is NOT what I signed up for! In tree calculus all lambdas are encoded as trees and binders are encoded as like sequences of S/K combinators that wrap a given subtree (much overhead, not ideal) but at least you can have a single primitive rule (emulated by a sequence of ic reduction steps) that can implement introspection on a sub tree. It seems to be a much harder problem when the association between binder and variable is done via edge in a graph—as how does one case-analysis on a graph via local rewrite rules exactly? It's even more weird when everything needs to be linear by default. I was somehow able to get linear to work in like a version of the tree calculus that had 9 rules but it was still kinda weird, and obv had tc bracket abstraction overhead. I think I'm going to just keep prompting here and see if I can either get it to strait up solve the problem of introspection overhead (it tried with a "table" node, I vetoed this as well) or perhaps switch to a version of interaction nets where signal can flow along the wires themselves to be like closer to an FPGA spiritually🤔

Reflective nets, reducing



  
    
    
loading…



    
      
        

      
      
        ⏮
        ◀◀
        ◀
        ▶
        ▶▶
        ⏭
        
         a round at a time
      

      
        order
          all at once, in roundsnewest pair firstrandom
         variable wires
         fold named parts
         subnets
         physical
         motion
         follow
      

    

  

  
    Reflective nets, reducing

    Click a bright wire, or either agent on it, to fire that pair. ▶ steps in the order chosen
      under the bar. Drag the bar to scrub through the run, either way. Hold Shift to light up the
      whole subnet under the pointer.

    Pointed at

    point at an agent

    The net as a term, now

    

    The rule

    point at a bright wire, or follow a link above

    Now

    

    Try

    

    The adds

    Every add in the prelude, named for the kind of program it is, the shape of its numbers and the way
      it adds. Click one to play it.

    linear uses every variable, so no eraser ever appears, and copies
      only where a variable is used twice. ordinary is the usual way: a
      fixpoint or a test, and what is not picked is erased. reversible
      is linear and also hands the first number back, so a subtract can undo the add: an add alone
      forgets, since 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 give one sum.

    

    What you are looking at

    A λ-calculus run as an interaction net. Each shape is an agent, each line a wire. Two agents
      joined by their main ports (a bright wire, in the colour of what the rewrite will do) are about
      to rewrite; nothing else can happen. The program hangs from the root (the ring at the top), and its
      answer ends up there.

    Structures. Code that hangs together sits on one faint band: one value, or one stretch of
      code. Bands keep apart, and what is running, copying or erasing stands between them. A band's label
      is the name of the definition it comes from, or else the start of its term. A number carries
      a green tag that says which number it is, wherever it is and however it was built; its bits are
      the parts named b0 and b1.

    Terms. Point at an agent to read the subnet under it as a term, and see the whole net as one
      above. A name stands for a definition that is whole. In a term, ▸c is a thaw on code c,
      f @ a an application that is running, ‹v› a value a variable holds,
      ⧉n⟨v⟩ a side of copy n that has still to pass through v, and ρ⟨v⟩ a read
      under way.

    Physical. Tick it and play: the two agents of every pair that can fire are drawn together,
      and the pair rewrites when its main pins touch. What is close goes first, and what must cross the
      net goes later. The answer and the number of rewrites are the same as in any other order.

    Ports. Every port is a pin on its own side of the icon, and wires join pin tips. The main
      port's pin ends in a white dot. Only main ports meet: a rewrite happens where two main ports
      are wired together, and it rewires what was on the side ports. An icon turns, and flips left
      for right, to face its pins toward what they are wired to; its letter stays upright.

    Named parts. The code of a definition (suc, size, …) that nothing is acting on is
      drawn as its name on a pill. Click a pill to open it, and the tag of an opened part to fold it
      again. A part opens by itself when a thaw, a copier or an eraser reaches it, and its copies fold
      when they are whole.

    Drag an agent to move it; the layout gives way around it and settles again when you let go.
      Drag empty space to move the view, and scroll to zoom.

    Code is frozen. The grey shapes are code: functions (λ on a tile), applications (small disks) and
      uses of variables (dots). Code does nothing by itself. A thaw (green arrow) walks down it and
      turns each application into a running one (pink @). A thaw stops at a function: the body stays
      frozen until the function is called, so nothing inside a body ever moves early.

    A call is a running application meeting a function. The argument is wired to the uses of the
      variable (the thin violet wires), and a thaw starts on the body.

    Copying happens only where a variable is used twice: a split (thin violet Y) sits on its wire.
      When a value arrives, copiers (thick Y, one colour per copy) walk through it one agent at a
      time, and cancel where the two ends of one copy meet. Two copies under way at once keep their
      own colours: watch that a cancel always joins one colour.

    Erasing happens only where a variable is not used: an eraser (red ×) walks through the value.

    Reading: ρ v makes a reader (ρ on a cyan disk). It builds a function of five arms and
      hands the value's parts to the arm for its kind: function, opened function, application, captured
      value, or ρ. Reading a function opens it (Λ on an open tile): applied, an opened function hands
      back its body as code instead of running it. Reading it again closes it.

    The shapes named here are the suggested icons; others can be chosen.

    Linear programs (linear_unary_add, linear_list_add) use every variable,
      so no eraser ever appears, and the only copies are the ones the program asks for: a number is its own
      loop, each successor copies the step once, and zero hands the last copy back. Try
      linear_unary_add 40u 2u or linear_list_add 1000 2000, with numbers of any size: the
      answer holds the sum first, then what is handed back.

    Numbers as trees. 1014t is a tree of bits: pairs of pairs with a bit at each leaf,
      the low half on the left, and beside it the depth as a loop. linear_tree_add 1014t 2413t
      adds two of them with nothing erased, and hands back a tree: the adder for a tree is two adders for
      its halves, and the depth says how often to halve. ordinary_tree_add adds the same trees
      the usual way, testing each bit and dropping the arm not taken. linear_tree_add_parallel
      adds them in parallel and still erases nothing: every part of a tree works out its carry out for
      both carries in at once, and the carry then goes down. Played a round at a time, it takes 85 more
      rounds for each doubling of the trees, where linear_tree_add takes twice the rounds. A
      number that is folded opens when you click it; &open=1 in the link starts with the
      numbers open.

    Reversible. A linear add erases nothing and still forgets: many pairs of numbers give one
      sum. reversible_tree_add a b hands back a and the sum, and
      reversible_tree_sub a s hands back a and s − a, so each undoes the
      other: reversible_tree_add 1014t 2413t reversible_tree_sub ends with 1014 and 2413 again.
      Only the answers can be had back this way. A rewrite of the net cannot be undone: the ◀ buttons go
      back to moments the page kept.

    Order does not matter. Fire pairs in any order you like, or pick another order under the bar:
      the answer is the same, and so is the number of rewrites. A pair you fire replaces what was
      planned from that moment; the rest of the run is planned again, and its length does not change.

    Rewrites

    

    Agents

    

    Choose other icons: four ways to draw each agent, and what each agent really does.

    Writing programs

    \x y. body is a function, ^x. body an opened one (so (^d. p) u is the code
      of p), f a applies, ρ reads. Every name must be bound by a function or
      defined: name := term; … defines names first. A number is written with its form after its digits. The linear ones:
      5u is unary, 5 a list of bits and 5t a tree of bits. The ordinary
      ones: 5s is unary and 5c a list of bits. For the add whose two numbers have
      different shapes, 5a is a number whose cells pick an arm and 5p a chain of
      pairs. Every list of bits in a program gets one bit more than the largest needs, so a sum of two
      fits, and every tree number the fewest levels that hold as much. A value that is such a number is
      shown as one, and a tree of bits with no depth beside it as {n|leaves}. These are defined
      already:

    zero, suc, add, true, false, Z, kindOf, size, no, err, close, open, interp, and the adds:
      linear_unary_add, ordinary_unary_add, linear_list_add, linear_list_add_two_shapes, ordinary_list_add,
      linear_tree_add, ordinary_tree_add, linear_tree_add_parallel, ordinary_tree_add_parallel,
      reversible_tree_add, reversible_tree_sub, reversible_tree_add_parallel, reversible_tree_sub_parallel,
      with their parts

    The design: DESIGN.md; its theorems: PATHWAY.md.
      The engine here is engine.js, held to the Python nets by check.mjs.
